strengths: Interesting and creative core idea: procedurally generating simple 'Cézanne toy' primitives (spheres, cuboids, cylinders, rings) as a scalable, cheap training distribution for grasping, motivated by developmental psychology.

Extensive empirical validation across simulation and two distinct real robot embodiments (Franka arm with parallel gripper, Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands), with consistent gains over strong VLA baselines (OpenVLA-OFT, π0-FAST) despite orders of magnitude less data and a much smaller model (86M vs 3B/7B parameters).

Thorough ablation studies: pooling mechanism (DetPool vs attention/CLS/mean pooling), model size, number/diversity of toys vs number of demonstrations, importance of individual primitives, toy complexity, and color diversity — these provide good insight into what drives generalization.

Reasonably clear architecture description and detailed appendices (toy manufacturing process, hardware configurations, training hyperparameters, baseline implementation details, evaluation protocols) that aid reproducibility.

Results engage directly with a real and practically important problem (zero-shot generalization in manipulation) and offer a scalable, low-cost data-generation recipe that could be useful to the community.
weaknesses: LEGO's DetPool mechanism relies on test-time object segmentation masks (via SAM2 or a trained detector), essentially providing privileged object-localization information that the baseline VLA models do not receive; this makes the comparison to π0-FAST/OpenVLA-OFT somewhat unequal and complicates the 'zero-shot generalization' narrative, since success partly hinges on a separate, non-trivial perception module rather than the policy itself.

Evaluation is restricted to a single skill (pick-and-lift grasping) with a coarse success criterion (lifting above a height threshold); it remains unclear whether the object-centric representation and toy-based training generalize to more dexterous, contact-rich, or multi-step manipulation tasks.

Some baseline results appear weak relative to expectations (e.g., OpenVLA-OFT degrading with more data, π0-FAST needing large in-domain finetuning to be competitive), raising questions about whether baselines were optimally tuned; the paper's own explanation (overfitting, domain gap) is plausible but not deeply diagnosed.

The scaling and ablation studies, while useful, are conducted only in simulation, leaving open whether the same trends (e.g., diminishing returns from more demos vs. toy diversity) hold in the real-world settings where the headline results are reported.

Limited discussion of failure modes and error analysis (e.g., what kinds of real objects the model fails on, or how sensitive results are to segmentation mask quality/errors), which would strengthen understanding of the method's robustness limits.

The main contribution (a compositional-primitive dataset generation strategy plus attention-masked pooling) is somewhat incremental relative to existing object-centric representation literature (e.g., OTTER), and the paper's positioning against that closest related work is fairly brief.

strengths: The central idea—training grasping policies exclusively on procedurally generated primitive-based 'toys' and testing zero-shot on real YCB objects—is a creative and well-motivated testbed for studying generalization, inspired by developmental psychology.

The experimental scope is broad: simulation (ManiSkill), two real robot embodiments (Franka+Robotiq gripper, Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands), and multiple baselines (OpenVLA-OFT, π0-FAST, ShapeGrasp).

Reasonably thorough ablations are provided (pooling mechanism, model size, toy diversity vs. number of demos, individual primitive importance, toy complexity, color diversity), which help probe what factors drive generalization.

The appendix provides substantial reproducibility detail (toy primitive dimension ranges, 3D-printing settings, hardware configurations, teleoperation protocols, training hyperparameters), which is commendable.
The DetPool mechanism is a clean, lightweight idea (attention masking + mean pooling within a ViT) that is simple to implement and plausibly transferable to other pretrained vision backbones.
weaknesses: Comparisons with VLA baselines appear confounded: LEGO relies on an explicit per-frame object segmentation mask (via a Faster R-CNN detector trained on 200 annotated toy images plus SAM2) to tell the policy exactly which object to attend to, which is privileged/oracle-like information not available to OpenVLA-OFT or π0-FAST. This makes it unclear whether gains stem from the proposed training data/method or simply from supplying ground-truth-like localization at test time, undermining the central claim that object-centric representations learned via DetPool are the 'key' to generalization.

It is unclear how the toy-trained object detector generalizes to detect/segment the 64 diverse, out-of-distribution real YCB test objects at inference time; no evaluation of detector accuracy on these novel objects is reported, leaving a critical pipeline component unvalidated.

The paper's own Table 2 shows that finetuned π0-FAST (76.56%) clearly outperforms LEGO (66.67%) on the real Franka/YCB benchmark, yet the abstract and conclusion claim LEGO 'outperforms state-of-the-art approaches' and 'significantly outperforms' VLA models—this is an overclaim relative to the actual second-place result, which is only clarified deep in the body text.

The real-world evaluation scale is limited, especially for the H1-2 humanoid experiments (13 objects × 5 trials = 65 total trials per method), which is too small to draw statistically reliable conclusions; no confidence intervals or variance are reported anywhere.

The scope of the task is restricted to simple single-step pick-and-lift grasping; no evidence is given that the object-centric representation or toy-based training generalizes to more complex manipulation (e.g., placement, insertion, multi-step tasks), despite the broad framing of 'generalizable manipulation' in the introduction.

Novelty of the core architectural contribution (DetPool) is incremental: masked attention + pooling for object-centric features is conceptually similar to prior object-centric approaches (e.g., OTTER, cited by the authors), and the primary distinguishing claim rests on an engineering/data-generation choice rather than a fundamentally new representation-learning technique.

Minor inconsistencies in narrative versus data (e.g., claim that 'sphere is the most critical primitive' is only true in 3 of 4 demo-count settings in Table 4, with cuboid removal giving the worst result at 100 demos) suggest the analysis/writing was not fully double-checked.

strengths: Creative and well-motivated core idea: generating a systematic, scalable training distribution ('Cézanne toys') from four primitive shapes to study zero-shot generalization in grasping, drawing a nice connection to developmental psychology.

Broad and fairly rigorous empirical evaluation spanning simulation (ManiSkill/YCB), a real Franka+Robotiq gripper setup, and a real Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands, demonstrating the approach generalizes across embodiments.
The proposed DetPool mechanism is clearly motivated and empirically validated against reasonable pooling alternatives (mean, CLS, attention pooling), showing consistent and sizable gains.

Extensive ablation and scaling studies (toy diversity vs. number of demonstrations, model size, primitive-type importance, toy complexity, color diversity) that provide useful insight into what drives generalization, going beyond a single headline result.

Strong efficiency story: an 86M-parameter model trained from scratch on a small toy dataset is competitive with or better than much larger pretrained VLA baselines (π0-FAST 3B, OpenVLA-OFT 7B) in most settings.

Good documentation/reproducibility effort in the appendix (toy generation scripts, printer settings, hardware configurations, teleoperation protocols, baseline fine-tuning details, evaluation protocols).
weaknesses: The headline claim of outperforming state-of-the-art approaches is weakened by the real Franka results (Table 2), where the fine-tuned π0-FAST actually beats LEGO (76.56% vs 66.67%); the paper frames this as 'second-best' but the comparison muddies the central generalization claim and deserves more careful, balanced discussion rather than being relegated to a short explanatory paragraph.

DetPool depends on an external object detector/segmenter (a custom-trained Faster R-CNN + SAM2) at inference time for real-world images; the quality and generalization of this upstream detection pipeline to truly novel objects is not stress-tested or ablated (e.g., failure cases, sensitivity to detector errors), even though it is central to the claimed object-centric generalization.

Evaluation is restricted to single-step pick-and-lift grasping with a simple lift-height success criterion; no assessment of grasp quality, stability under perturbation, or more complex manipulation, and this narrow scope is only acknowledged briefly as future work.

Sample sizes per object are small (16 trials per object in simulation/Franka, only 5 trials per object on H1-2), and no variance/confidence intervals are reported, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of reported success-rate differences, especially for closely matched methods.

Baseline comparisons may be somewhat unfair to large pretrained VLA models, which are fine-tuned on the same very small toy dataset as LEGO; such large models are known to be data-hungry and may be undertrained in this regime, which could partly explain their weaker performance rather than solely demonstrating the superiority of the object-centric representation.
The H1-2 dexterous-hand evaluation was limited in scope due to hardware issues (unresponsive thumb joints), reducing confidence in the generality of the dexterous-hand results.

Limited theoretical or mechanistic explanation for why masking attention to object patches specifically (versus other forms of object-centric conditioning) is the key ingredient; the explanation remains primarily empirical/ablation-based.

strengths: Interesting and well-motivated research question inspired by developmental cognitive science: can a robot policy generalize to novel real-world objects after training only on simple, randomly composed 'toy' primitives (spheres, cuboids, cylinders, rings)? The framing and the constructed 'Cezanne toys' dataset is a creative and potentially useful contribution to the community.

The proposed DetPool mechanism (masking ViT attention to object patches, then mean-pooling object tokens) is simple, lightweight, and clearly explained, and is shown via ablation to be substantially better than attention/CLS/mean pooling baselines across a wide range of demo counts (Table 1).

Extensive empirical evaluation across three platforms (ManiSkill simulation, Franka+Robotiq gripper on YCB, Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands), with comparisons to strong, much larger pretrained baselines (pi0-FAST 3B, OpenVLA-OFT 7B) and additional object-centric baselines (ShapeGrasp, GROOT, DexGraspVLA).

Numerous informative ablation/scaling studies: number and diversity of training toys, model size, primitive-type importance, toy complexity, geometric similarity (Chamfer distance) between train/test objects, condition/prediction horizon, delta vs absolute control, and color diversity.
A dedicated robustness study (lighting, clutter, distractors, mask noise) strengthens the claim that the object-centric representation is not brittle.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendices on toy manufacturing (printer settings), hardware configurations, teleoperation protocols, and baseline implementation/hyperparameters.

The core claim of data efficiency (86M-parameter model trained from scratch on 1.5K real demos matching or beating multi-billion-parameter VLAs in zero-shot settings) is a meaningful and practically relevant finding for the field.
weaknesses: The abstract's claim of 'outperforming state-of-the-art approaches' is partially overstated: on the real Franka benchmark (Table 2), the finetuned pi0-FAST actually beats LEGO (76.56% vs 66.67%), a fact only clarified in the body text, not reflected in the abstract framing.

The method's practical 'zero-shot' generalization depends on an external object segmentation/detection pipeline (SAM2 in the real world, or a separately trained Faster R-CNN detector for bounding boxes) to identify the target object at inference time. This adds a non-trivial dependency that is not deeply analyzed (e.g., failure cases when detection is wrong on truly novel objects) and somewhat complicates the 'grasp anything zero-shot' narrative.

Core technical novelty is incremental: DetPool is a masked-attention + mean-pooling variant conceptually similar to prior object-centric approaches (e.g., OTTER, cited as most similar); the main novelty is largely empirical/dataset-driven rather than algorithmic.

Most quantitative results (simulation and real-robot tables) are reported as single numbers without variance/confidence intervals or multiple seeds, except for Table 6; given real-robot trials are limited (16 or fewer per object), this limits statistical confidence in reported success-rate differences, especially the narrow margins in some baseline comparisons.

Baseline comparisons are not fully matched in training/pretraining budget (e.g., pi0-FAST pretrained on large-scale pi/DROID data vs LEGO trained from scratch), which is acknowledged but still makes some 'outperforming SOTA' claims less like-for-like, since the comparison conflates architecture, pretraining scale, and fine-tuning data simultaneously.

Task diversity is narrow: nearly all experiments are single-object pick/lift grasping (plus one push-to-target task in the appendix); the generalization claims are therefore scoped to grasping and not validated on more complex or long-horizon manipulation.
The H1-2 dexterous-hand evaluation was limited in scope due to hardware issues (unresponsive thumb joints), reducing confidence in the humanoid generalization claims relative to the Franka results.

The paper does not discuss failure modes or qualitative analysis of when/why the object-centric representation fails to generalize (e.g., which YCB objects failed and why), which would strengthen understanding of the method's limits beyond the 'easy/medium/hard' Chamfer-distance bucketing.

strengths: Interesting and well-motivated central question (can robots generalize via training on simple composable 'toy' primitives, drawing analogy to developmental psychology), executed with a concrete, reproducible data-generation pipeline (procedural toy generation + 3D printing).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning simulation (ManiSkill/YCB), two distinct real robot embodiments (Franka arm with parallel gripper, Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands), and a push-to-target task beyond grasping.

Thorough ablation studies: pooling mechanism comparisons (DetPool vs. attention/CLS/mean pooling), primitive-type importance, toy complexity, model size, condition/prediction length, delta vs. absolute control, and color diversity.
Additional robustness analyses in the appendix (lighting, clutter, distractors, mask noise) that strengthen confidence in the method's practical resilience.

Comparisons against a reasonably broad set of relevant baselines (OpenVLA-OFT, π0-FAST, ShapeGrasp, GROOT, DexGraspVLA), and good documentation of implementation details (hardware configs, training hyperparameters, print settings) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution (DetPool) is a relatively simple combination of segmentation-mask-restricted attention plus mean pooling; conceptually it is close to prior object-centric representation work (e.g., OTTER, GROOT) and the novelty over masked/region pooling techniques in vision is incremental.

The 'zero-shot' generalization narrative is weakened by the method's dependence on an external, separately trained perception pipeline (SAM2 in simulation with GT masks, and a Faster R-CNN detector trained on 200 manually annotated toy images for real-world deployment). Much of the apparent generalization burden may be carried by this external detector/segmenter rather than the policy itself, and its own generalization to truly novel objects/scenes is not independently evaluated.

In the real Franka experiment (Table 2), the finetuned π0-FAST baseline actually outperforms LEGO (76.56% vs. 66.67%), which directly contradicts the paper's central claim of outperforming SOTA; this result is downplayed in the text ('second-best') despite undermining the headline contribution.

Success criterion is a simple lift-above-threshold metric; it does not assess grasp quality, stability under perturbation, placement, or longer-horizon task completion, which limits the practical significance of the reported success rates.

Trial counts are modest for some settings (e.g., only 5 trials per object for the H1-2 experiments, 16 grid placements for Franka/simulation), and statistical significance (confidence intervals) is reported only for one ablation (Table 6), making it hard to assess whether many reported differences (e.g., between pooling variants) are robust.

Baseline training/tuning details raise fairness concerns: baselines are given limited fine-tuning steps and ad hoc early-stopping heuristics (e.g., π0-FAST checkpoint selection to avoid overfitting) rather than a systematic hyperparameter search, which could understate their true achievable performance relative to the heavily-tuned proposed method.

Evaluation scope is narrow relative to the title's broad claim ('grasp anything'): only tested on YCB objects and a 13-object everyday set, with simple pick-up behavior; generalization to deformable, thin, transparent, or highly irregular objects is not explored, so the title/abstract claims arguably overreach the evidence provided.

strengths: Interesting and well-motivated central idea: training grasping policies on randomly-composed 'Cézanne toys' built from four shape primitives, inspired by developmental psychology, as a path to zero-shot generalization on real-world objects.

Broad and thorough experimental validation: results are reported in simulation (ManiSkill) and on two distinct real embodiments (Franka arm + Robotiq gripper, and a Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands), lending credibility to the generalization claims.

Extensive ablation studies covering pooling mechanism (DetPool vs. attention/CLS/mean pooling), model size, number/diversity of training toys, number of demonstrations, primitive type importance, toy complexity, toy color, control parameterization (absolute vs. delta), and condition/prediction horizon length.

Strong comparisons against relevant and larger baselines (OpenVLA-OFT, π0-FAST, ShapeGrasp, GROOT, DexGraspVLA), showing LEGO achieves competitive or superior zero-shot performance with an 86M-parameter model trained on a small, synthetic dataset versus billion-parameter models pretrained on large-scale robot data.

Good supplementary robustness analyses (lighting, clutter, distractors, mask noise) and reproducibility-oriented appendices (toy manufacturing details, print settings, hardware configurations, training hyperparameters).

Clear practical significance: demonstrates that strong generalization in grasping can emerge from small, cheaply generated synthetic data rather than costly large-scale real-world pretraining, which could meaningfully lower the barrier for manipulation research.
weaknesses: The central comparison is undercut on the real Franka setup, where finetuned π0-FAST actually outperforms LEGO (76.56% vs 66.67%); the paper's narrative emphasizes LEGO's superiority but the strongest real-robot number is actually a baseline, which should be more prominently and critically discussed rather than relegated to an explanatory aside.

DetPool depends on test-time object segmentation (via SAM2 or a custom-trained Faster R-CNN detector) to know which patches belong to the target object; this adds an external dependency and potential failure mode (e.g., in cluttered or ambiguous scenes) that is not fully costed into the method's claimed simplicity or robustness, despite the mask-noise ablation attempting to address this.

Task diversity is narrow: nearly all evaluation is single-object pick-up/lifting (with one brief push-to-target experiment in the appendix); claims of 'generalizable dexterous manipulation' may be overstated relative to the actual scope of tasks tested.

Statistical reporting is thin for the main results (Tables 1-3): most numbers are single point estimates without confidence intervals or variance across seeds, and real-world trial counts are modest (16 per object for Franka, only 5 per object for H1-2 across 13 objects), making it hard to assess the robustness/significance of reported differences, especially for close calls (e.g., LEGO vs. attention pooling baseline in simulation).

Fairness of baseline tuning is unclear: the large pretrained VLA baselines (OpenVLA-OFT, π0-FAST) are finetuned with settings and training budgets chosen by the authors, and claims that these models 'overfit' or are 'too data-hungry' are largely hypothesized rather than rigorously diagnosed with systematic hyperparameter/regularization sweeps for the baselines.

The core technical novelty (restricting ViT attention to object patches via a segmentation mask, then mean-pooling) is a relatively incremental combination of existing object-centric representation ideas (e.g., OTTER, prior masked/attention pooling approaches), with the primary novelty residing more in the toy-generation data strategy than in the architectural contribution.

The H1-2 humanoid evaluation is limited (13 objects, 5 trials each, only left arm/hand used due to hardware issues with the Inspire hand's thumb joints), which weakens the strength of the multi-embodiment generalization claims for that platform.
